slides: Start with one generator, G1, alone on its own load. Whatever the load asks for, G1 must supply.
The governor on the prime mover senses only shaft speed. When the load slows the shaft, it opens the valve in proportion to the fall in speed.
Watch the load rise from zero to one hundred megawatts. The operating point slides down the line, from sixty-one hertz at no load to fifty-nine point two two hertz at full load.
That fall in speed, as a percentage of full-load speed, is the speed droop: three percent for G1. The slope, s P, is fifty-six point three megawatts per hertz.
Raise the droop to five percent and the line steepens. A small droop means a flat line and a stiff unit: many megawatts for each hertz.
Raise the set point and the whole line slides up. The same load is now carried at a higher frequency. Alone, though, a heavily loaded unit cannot hold sixty hertz.
Now connect G1 to the infinite bus. The grid holds the frequency at sixty hertz, whatever G1 does.
G1's power is where its droop line crosses the sixty hertz line. At a set point of sixty-one hertz, that is fifty-six point three megawatts.
Raise the set point to sixty-one point four two hertz. G1's power rises to eighty megawatts, and the bus supplies twenty-three point seven megawatts less.
On the bus, the frequency does not move. The set point decides the power.
Lower the set point below sixty hertz and the power turns negative. The bus now drives G1 as a motor, and a reverse-power relay trips it.
Now three unlike units share one isolated load, with no bus to hold the frequency.
Each unit has its own set point and its own droop, so each has its own line. All three must run at one frequency.
The frequency settles where the three outputs add up to the load. At one hundred fifty megawatts that is sixty point one four hertz.
G1 carries forty-eight point three, G2 fifty-seven point four, and G3 forty-four point three megawatts.
Now step the load up sixty megawatts. The frequency falls to fifty-nine point seven eight hertz, and each unit picks up a share in proportion to its s P.
G3, the stiffest unit, takes the most: twenty-four point four megawatts. G2, with the largest droop, takes the least.
At two hundred ten megawatts the frequency sits at fifty-nine point seven eight hertz. Droop alone will never bring it back to sixty.
An operator, or automatic control, must move a set point. Here we raise G3's set point from sixty point eight to sixty-one point three four hertz.
G3's line shifts up, parallel to itself. Its slope does not change.
G3 now carries ninety point three megawatts. G1 drops to fifty-six point three and G2 to sixty-three point four.
And the frequency is back at sixty hertz. Moving set points is how operators restore the frequency.
A worked case. The load is one hundred eighty megawatts, with the set points as before.
Add the slopes: s P totals one hundred sixty-six point zero megawatts per hertz.
The system frequency is fifty-nine point nine six hertz. G1 carries fifty-eight point four, G2 sixty-five point zero, and G3 fifty-six point five megawatts; together, one hundred eighty.
To restore sixty hertz with G1 alone, the other two units are fixed by their lines at sixty hertz: sixty-three point four and fifty-four point zero megawatts. So G1 must carry sixty-two point six.
That needs G1's set point at sixty-one point one one hertz: sixty hertz plus sixty-two point six divided by fifty-six point three.
For one unit: the speed droop, the full-load frequency, the slope s P, and the power on its line.
For units in parallel: the load is the sum of the outputs, which gives the system frequency, and a load step is shared in proportion to s P.
On the infinite bus, the frequency is fixed and the set point decides the power.
lab: This is the Lab. Three units share the load; set the load, each set point and each droop.
Watch the warnings: a unit above one hundred megawatts is over its rating, and a unit below zero would motor.
Switch to the infinite bus to connect G1 alone to the grid at sixty hertz.
exp: Experiment one. At one hundred fifty megawatts, raise G3's droop to five percent, then step the load by sixty megawatts. How does G3's share change?
Experiment two. Set the load to two hundred forty megawatts. Can any single set point restore sixty hertz without a unit going over one hundred megawatts?
Experiment three. On the infinite bus, find the set point at which G1 carries no power. What happens below it?
Experiment four. Start at one hundred fifty megawatts and raise the load. Which unit reaches one hundred megawatts first, and at what load?
Experiment five, your turn. The load is two hundred forty megawatts. Predict first: will the frequency be above or below sixty hertz? Then find the system frequency and each unit's output.
